trans.sense: sum of money paid for instruction
training or instruction provided by a teacher or tutor

examples.text: Imagine a country where children do nothing but play until they start compulsory schooling at age seven. Then, without exception, they attend comprehensives until the age of 16.[…]There are no inspectors, no exams until the age of 18, no school league tables, no private tuition industry, no school uniforms. […]
examples.ref: 2013 July 19, Peter Wilby, “Finland spreads word on schools”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 6, page 30:

raw_glosses: (Ireland, UK) The training or instruction provided by a teacher or tutor.
glosses: The training or instruction provided by a teacher or tutor.

examples.text: Tuition in the past was like taking medicine and you sent children for it only if they were doing poorly in a subject.
examples.ref: 2021 August 18, Qiu Guanhua, “Forum: Heavy reliance on tuition to boost performance is not healthy”, in The Straits Times, Singapore, archived from the original on 28 Dec 2022:

raw_glosses: (India, Malaysia, Singapore, Australia) Paid private classes taken outside of formal education; tutoring. (also used attributively)
glosses: Paid private classes taken outside of formal education; tutoring. (also used attributively)

examples.text: The school’s tuition will increase by five percent next year.

raw_glosses: (Canada, US, Philippines) A sum of money paid for instruction (such as in a private school, boarding school, university, or college).
glosses: A sum of money paid for instruction (such as in a private school, boarding school, university, or college).

examples.text:
BENEDICK. I have almost matter enough in me for such an embassage; and so I commit you—
CLAUDIO. To the tuition of God: from my house, if I had it,—
DON PEDRO. The sixth of July: your loving friend, Benedick.
BENEDICK. Nay, mock not, mock not.
